title: Ὅρκια καὶ ἔγχεα
titleEn: The Oaths and the Spear-Casts — Iliad 3.264–368
about: The sacrifice for the oaths is made on the plain. Agamemnon and Odysseus rise, the heralds mix the wine and pour water over the kings’ hands, and Agamemnon cuts hair from the lambs’ heads, which is shared among the leaders. He prays to Zeus, the Sun, the rivers, the earth and the powers below, and states the terms: if Alexander kills Menelaus, he keeps Helen and the possessions and the Achaeans sail home; if Menelaus kills him, the Trojans give Helen back and pay a recompense; and if they refuse, Agamemnon will go on fighting. He cuts the lambs’ throats, and both armies pour wine and pray that whoever breaks the oaths may have his brain run out like the wine and his wives be given to others. Zeus does not yet fulfil the prayer. Priam, who cannot bear to watch his son fight, puts the lambs in his chariot and drives back to Ilios with Antenor. Hector and Odysseus measure the ground and shake lots in a helmet, and Paris’ lot leaps out first. The two champions arm, Alexander in the breastplate of his brother Lycaon, and march into the middle. Alexander throws first, but his spear bends back in Menelaus’ shield. Menelaus prays for vengeance and throws: the spear goes through Paris’ shield and breastplate and cuts his tunic, but Paris leans aside and escapes. Menelaus strikes at the helmet, and his sword breaks into pieces. He cries out to Zeus that no god is deadlier.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκοντο μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς,
ἐξ ἵππων ἀποβάντες ἐπὶ χθόνα πουλυβότειραν
ἐς μέσσον Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ἐστιχόωντο.
sentences.i: But when they had come among the Trojans and the Achaeans, they stepped down from their horses onto the earth that feeds so many and marched into the middle, between the Trojans and the Achaeans.
sentences.n: The two who left the city at the end of the last part, Priam and Antenor, have reached the plain, and the sacrifice for the oaths can begin. ἵκοντο is a past tense of ἱκνέομαι ‘come, arrive’, and ἐξ ἵππων ‘from the horses’ means down from the chariot; ἀποβάντες is the aorist participle of ἀποβαίνω ‘step down’. πουλυβότειραν ‘much-nourishing’ is the stock epithet of the earth, translated the same way every time. ἐστιχόωντο, the imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘march in line’ (from στίχες ‘ranks’), has its vowels left uncontracted; the line 266 returns word for word at 341 for the two champions.

sentences.t:
ὄρνυτο δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων,
ἂν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς πολύμητις·
sentences.l:
And rose at once thereupon the lord of men, Agamemnon,
and up Odysseus, many-wiled;
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, rose at once, and Odysseus of many wiles rose with him;
sentences.n: The two leaders who will conduct the oath stand up, Agamemnon for the Achaeans and Odysseus beside him. ὄρνυτο is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, so ‘roused himself, rose’; ἂν δ’ is ἀνά ‘up’ with the verb left to be understood from the line before, and not the particle ἄν. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ and πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ are stock epithets, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ κήρυκες ἀγαυοὶ
ὅρκια πιστὰ θεῶν σύναγον, κρητῆρι δὲ οἶνον
μίσγον, ἀτὰρ βασιλεῦσιν ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν.
sentences.l:
and the heralds, noble ones,
the faithful oaths of the gods brought together, and in the mixing-bowl wine
they mingled, and for the kings water over their hands they poured.
sentences.i: And the noble heralds brought together the faithful oaths of the gods, mixed wine in the mixing-bowl, and poured water over the kings’ hands.
sentences.n: The heralds prepare what the oath needs. ὅρκια πιστὰ θεῶν ‘the faithful oaths of the gods’ names the things that make the oath binding, the lambs and the wine, as at 245 in the last part; the wine is mixed in the κρητήρ ‘mixing-bowl’, and the water poured over the kings’ hands is the ritual washing before a sacrifice. κήρυκες ἀγαυοί ‘noble heralds’ is a stock phrase, and ἀγαυός is translated ‘noble’ every time. σύναγον and μίσγον are imperfects without the augment, and ἔχευαν is the aorist of χέω ‘pour’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ ἐρυσσάμενος χείρεσσι μάχαιραν,
ἥ οἱ πὰρ ξίφεος μέγα κουλεόν αἰὲν ἄωρτο,
ἀρνῶν ἐκ κεφαλέων τάμνε τρίχας·
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus drew with his hands the knife that always hung beside the great sheath of his sword, and cut hairs from the heads of the lambs;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is Agamemnon here; the same name is used of Menelaus later (Ἀτρεΐδαο at 347, Ἀτρεΐδης at 350), and each time the context says which. Cutting hair from the victims’ heads is the first act of the sacrifice, and the hairs are shared out in the next lines. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw (from the sheath)’, with the dative of the hands; the μάχαιρα is a knife, kept apart in English from the ξίφος ‘sword’ whose sheath it hangs beside. ἄωρτο is the pluperfect passive of ἀείρω ‘lift, hang up’, ‘had been hung up’, so ‘was hanging’, and κεφαλέων is the epic genitive plural of κεφαλή.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
κήρυκες Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν νεῖμαν ἀρίστοις.
sentences.l:
but then
the heralds of the Trojans and Achaeans dealt them out to the best men.
sentences.i: and then the heralds of the Trojans and of the Achaeans dealt them out to the best men.
sentences.n: The hairs just cut are shared out among the leaders of both armies. The Greek gives the verb no object; ‘them’ is supplied from τρίχας ‘hairs’ in the line before. νεῖμαν is the aorist of νέμω ‘distribute’, without the augment, and ἀρίστοις is ‘the best men’, the chiefs.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀτρεΐδης μεγάλ’ εὔχετο χεῖρας ἀνασχών·
sentences.l: And for them Atreus’-son loudly prayed, his hands raising:
sentences.i: On their behalf the son of Atreus raised his hands and prayed loudly:
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s prayer follows at once, and it is also the statement of the terms of the duel. τοῖσιν δ’ ‘and for them’ points to those just served with the hairs; μεγάλ’ εὔχετο is ‘prayed loudly’ (εὔχομαι is ‘pray’, not ‘boast’, here), and χεῖρας ἀνασχών ‘raising his hands’ is the gesture of prayer. Ἀτρεΐδης is Agamemnon again.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ Ἴδηθεν μεδέων κύδιστε μέγιστε,
Ἠέλιός θ’, ὃς πάντ’ ἐφορᾷς καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούεις,
καὶ ποταμοὶ καὶ γαῖα, καὶ οἳ ὑπένερθε καμόντας
ἀνθρώπους τίνυσθον ὅτις κ’ ἐπίορκον ὀμόσσῃ,
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, from Ida ruling, most glorious, greatest,
and Sun, you who oversee all things and listen to all things,
and rivers, and earth, and you who below men who have toiled
punish, whoever swears a false oath,
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious, greatest, and Sun, you who see everything and hear everything, and rivers, and earth, and you who below punish men whose toil is done, whoever swears a false oath,
sentences.n: Agamemnon calls on every power that can witness an oath: the sky-god, the Sun, the rivers, the earth, and those below. Ἴδηθεν is Ἴδη ‘Mount Ida’ with the suffix -θεν ‘from’, and μεδέων is the epic participle ‘ruling over’ (μέδω); κύδιστε μέγιστε ‘most glorious, greatest’ recurs as a pair at 298 and 320. ἐφορᾷς and ἐπακούεις are second-person forms of a half-line the Odyssey has in the third person, of the Sun who oversees and hears everything. καμόντας ἀνθρώπους ‘men who have toiled’ are the dead; τίνυσθον is a dual, so two powers below are meant, unnamed. The address runs on to the next unit.

sentences.t: ὑμεῖς μάρτυροι ἔστε, φυλάσσετε δ’ ὅρκια πιστά·
sentences.l: you be witnesses, and guard the faithful oaths:
sentences.i: be witnesses, and guard the faithful oaths:
sentences.n: The main verbs come at last: ἔστε is the imperative of εἰμί ‘be’ (‘be you’) and φυλάσσετε the imperative of φυλάσσω ‘guard’. The colon is ours, for the Greek has an ano teleia; the terms of the oath follow in three ‘if’-clauses.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κεν Μενέλαον Ἀλέξανδρος καταπέφνῃ
αὐτὸς ἔπειθ’ Ἑλένην ἐχέτω καὶ κτήματα πάντα,
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐν νήεσσι νεώμεθα ποντοπόροισιν·
sentences.i: If Alexander kills Menelaus, let him keep Helen and all the possessions for himself, and let us go back in our sea-crossing ships;
sentences.n: The first term of the oath. εἰ … κεν with a subjunctive is ‘if … should’, and καταπέφνῃ is the subjunctive of the epic aorist of the root φεν- ‘slay’, with κατά; ἐχέτω is the third-person imperative of ἔχω ‘have, hold’, and νεώμεθα the hortative ‘let us go back’ (νέομαι). Ἀλέξανδρος is the other name of Πάρις, who is named at 325; κτήματα ‘possessions’ are the goods at stake along with Helen. ποντοπόροισιν ‘sea-crossing’ is the stock epithet of ships.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ Ἀλέξανδρον κτείνῃ ξανθὸς Μενέλαος,
Τρῶας ἔπειθ’ Ἑλένην καὶ κτήματα πάντ’ ἀποδοῦναι,
τιμὴν δ’ Ἀργείοις ἀποτινέμεν ἥν τιν’ ἔοικεν,
ἥ τε καὶ ἐσσομένοισι μετ’ ἀνθρώποισι πέληται.
sentences.l:
but if fair-haired Menelaus should kill Alexander,
the Trojans then are to give back Helen and all the possessions,
and to the Argives to pay back a recompense such as is fitting,
which shall be among men yet to come as well.
sentences.i: But if fair-haired Menelaus kills Alexander, then the Trojans are to give Helen back with all the possessions, and to pay the Argives a recompense such as is fitting, one that will remain among men yet to come as well.
sentences.n: The second term, the mirror of the first. ἀποδοῦναι and ἀποτινέμεν are infinitives standing for commands (‘are to give back’, ‘are to pay back’), with Τρῶας as their subject; ἀποτινέμεν is the epic infinitive in -έμεν of ἀποτίνω. τιμή is here the price paid for a wrong, which is why it is ‘recompense’ and not ‘honour’; ἥν τιν’ ἔοικεν is ‘whatever is fitting’. πέληται is the subjunctive of πέλομαι ‘be’, and the Greek says only that the recompense shall be among men to come, which we take to mean that it lasts. ξανθός ‘fair-haired’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἂν ἐμοὶ τιμὴν Πρίαμος Πριάμοιό τε παῖδες
τίνειν οὐκ ἐθέλωσιν Ἀλεξάνδροιο πεσόντος,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ καὶ ἔπειτα μαχήσομαι εἵνεκα ποινῆς
αὖθι μένων, ἧός κε τέλος πολέμοιο κιχείω.
sentences.l:
But if for me the recompense Priam and the sons of Priam
are unwilling to pay, Alexander having fallen,
then I even afterward will fight for the sake of the requital,
staying here, until I find the end of the war.”
sentences.i: But if Priam and the sons of Priam are unwilling to pay me the recompense when Alexander has fallen, then I will go on fighting, even afterward, for the sake of the requital, staying here until I find the end of the war.”
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s last term covers the case where Troy, after losing its champion, still refuses to pay. The genitive absolute Ἀλεξάνδροιο πεσόντος means ‘Alexander having fallen’ (aorist participle of πίπτω); the epic genitive ending -οιο is Attic -ου. τιμήν ‘recompense’ comes back from 286, and ποινή ‘requital’ is the payment exacted for a wrong. ἧος is the epic ‘until’, and κιχείω is the aorist subjunctive of κιχάνω ‘find, come upon’; the English keeps ‘find’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ, καὶ ἀπὸ στομάχους ἀρνῶν τάμε νηλέϊ χαλκῷ·
sentences.l: He spoke, and the throats of the lambs he cut off with pitiless bronze;
sentences.i: So he said, and cut the lambs’ throats with the pitiless bronze;
sentences.n: The prayer is finished and the killing begins. ἦ καί, closing a speech and starting the action, is ‘he spoke, and’; ἦ is the old ‘he said’. ἀπὸ … τάμε is a tmesis, ἀποτάμνω ‘cut off’, with the aorist unaugmented; στομάχους are the throats (στόμαχος ‘gullet’). νηλέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with pitiless bronze’ is a stock phrase for the knife, and ‘bronze’ stands for the blade.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοὺς μὲν κατέθηκεν ἐπὶ χθονὸς ἀσπαίροντας
θυμοῦ δευομένους·
sentences.l:
and them indeed he set down upon the ground, gasping,
lacking life;
sentences.i: and set them down on the ground, gasping, lacking life;
sentences.n: The lambs are laid down dying. ἀσπαίροντας ‘gasping’ and θυμοῦ δευομένους ‘lacking life’ are both accusative plural participles agreeing with τούς; δεύομαι ‘lack, be in need of’ takes the genitive, and θυμός here is the life that leaves the body. The unit ends at a mid-line ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀπὸ γὰρ μένος εἵλετο χαλκός.
sentences.l: for the bronze took their might away.
sentences.i: for the bronze took their might away.
sentences.n: The reason, given at once. ἀπὸ … εἵλετο is a tmesis, ἀφαιρέομαι ‘take away’, and μένος is ‘might’, the fighting strength that makes a living creature move; the English keeps ‘might’ for μένος every time.

sentences.t:
οἶνον δ’ ἐκ κρητῆρος ἀφυσσόμενοι δεπάεσσιν
ἔκχεον, ἠδ’ εὔχοντο θεοῖς αἰειγενέτῃσιν.
sentences.l:
And wine from the mixing-bowl drawing in cups
they poured out, and they prayed to the gods, forever-born.
sentences.i: Drawing wine from the mixing-bowl in their cups, they poured it out, and prayed to the everlasting gods.
sentences.n: The pouring of wine is the libation that goes with the prayer. ἀφυσσόμενοι is the middle participle of ἀφύσσω ‘draw up (for oneself)’, δεπάεσσιν the epic dative plural of δέπας ‘cup’, and ἔκχεον ‘they poured out’. αἰειγενέτῃσιν ‘forever-born’ is an epithet of the gods, kept apart from θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες ‘the gods who are forever’, and it is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε·
sentences.l: And thus kept saying someone of the Achaeans and of the Trojans:
sentences.i: And thus would some man, Achaean or Trojan, say:
sentences.n: No one is named: the prayer that follows is the voice of both armies, one man after another. εἴπεσκεν is an iterative past tense built on the aorist stem of εἶπον, the -σκ- suffix giving ‘kept saying, would say’, and τις ‘someone’ with the genitive Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε takes in men of either side. The same line recurs at 319, with the same English.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ κύδιστε μέγιστε καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι
ὁππότεροι πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια πημήνειαν
ὧδέ σφ’ ἐγκέφαλος χαμάδις ῥέοι ὡς ὅδε οἶνος
αὐτῶν καὶ τεκέων, ἄλοχοι δ’ ἄλλοισι δαμεῖεν.
sentences.l:
“Zeus, most glorious, greatest, and you other immortal gods,
whichever of the two first, in breach of the oaths, do harm,
so may their brain flow to the ground, like this wine,
theirs and their children’s, and their wives be subdued to others.”
sentences.i: “Zeus, most glorious, greatest, and you other immortal gods, whichever side first does harm in breach of the oaths, may their brain run out on the ground like this wine, theirs and their children’s, and may their wives be made subject to other men.”
sentences.n: A curse on the oath-breaker, spoken in the form of a prayer. ῥέοι and δαμεῖεν are optatives of wish (‘may it flow … may they be subdued’), and πημήνειαν, inside the relative clause, is the optative that goes with them (‘whichever of the two should do harm’); ὁππότεροι ‘whichever of the two’ is plural because each side is a party. ὑπὲρ ὅρκια is ‘over the oaths’, that is, in breach of them, and πημαίνω is ‘do harm’. ὡς ὅδε οἶνος ‘like this wine’ points at the wine just poured, so that the curse acts out its image. ἐγκέφαλος is ‘brain’ in the singular, and ἄλοχοι … δαμεῖεν (aorist passive optative of δάμνημι ‘subdue’) says that their wives are to be made subject to others, that is, taken over by other men as captives.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαν, οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ σφιν ἐπεκραίαινε Κρονίων.
sentences.l: So they spoke, but not yet for them did the son of Cronus bring it to fulfilment.
sentences.i: So they spoke, but the son of Cronus did not yet fulfil it for them.
sentences.n: The narrator’s own comment, outside the speeches: Zeus does not yet grant what has been asked. ὣς ἔφαν is the plural ‘so they spoke’, and ἐπεκραίαινε is the imperfect of ἐπικραιαίνω ‘bring to fulfilment’; πώ ‘yet’ leaves open what comes later. The line is the one at 2.419, with ‘they’ and ‘for them’ in place of ‘he’ and ‘for him’.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l: And among them Dardanus’ descendant Priam a speech spoke:
sentences.i: And Priam, a descendant of Dardanus, spoke among them:
sentences.n: Priam speaks to the two armies. Δαρδανίδης is a patronymic that reaches back many generations, ‘descendant of Dardanus’ (Δάρδανος is the ancestor of the royal house of Troy), and not ‘son’. μετὰ … ἔειπε is a tmesis, μετεῖπον ‘spoke among’, with μῦθον ‘a speech’ as its object.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l: “Hear me, Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans:
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans:
sentences.n: The call for attention. κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with the genitive μευ ‘me’; ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ is a stock epithet of the Achaeans, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ἐγὼν εἶμι προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν
ἄψ, ἐπεὶ οὔ πω τλήσομ’ ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρᾶσθαι
μαρνάμενον φίλον υἱὸν ἀρηϊφίλῳ Μενελάῳ·
sentences.i: For my part, I am going back to windy Ilios, since I shall by no means endure to look with my eyes upon my dear son fighting Menelaus, dear to Ares;
sentences.n: Priam says he is leaving because he cannot watch the fight. ἤτοι ‘for my part’ is one word in the edition, and ἐγών is ἐγώ with a final ν. εἶμι is ‘I am going’ and ἄψ ‘back’; Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν is ‘windy Ilios’, ἠνεμόεις ‘windy’ being the epithet here. τλήσομ’ ‘I shall endure’ takes the infinitive ὁρᾶσθαι, the epic contracted middle of ὁράω ‘look’, and μαρνάμενον is ‘fighting’ with the dative ἀρηϊφίλῳ Μενελάῳ ‘with Ares-loved Menelaus’.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς μέν που τό γε οἶδε καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι
ὁπποτέρῳ θανάτοιο τέλος πεπρωμένον ἐστίν.
sentences.l:
Zeus doubtless this at least knows, and the other immortal gods,
for which of the two the end of death is fated.”
sentences.i: Zeus doubtless knows this, and the other immortal gods: for which of the two the end that death brings is fated.”
sentences.n: Priam leaves the outcome to the gods, who alone know it. που ‘doubtless’ makes the claim confident, and τό γε οἶδε ‘knows this at least’ points forward to the clause that follows. ὁπποτέρῳ ‘for which of the two’ is a dative, and πεπρωμένον ἐστίν, the perfect passive participle of πόρω ‘furnish, allot’ with ‘is’, means ‘has been allotted, is fated’. τέλος θανάτοιο is ‘the end of death’, the death that ends a man. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἐς δίφρον ἄρνας θέτο ἰσόθεος φώς,
ἂν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔβαιν’ αὐτός, κατὰ δ’ ἡνία τεῖνεν ὀπίσσω·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and the lambs into the chariot he put, a man equal to a god,
and up he mounted himself, and the reins he drew tight backward;
sentences.i: So he said, and put the lambs into the chariot, a man the equal of a god, and mounted himself, and drew the reins back tight;
sentences.n: Priam takes the dead lambs back with him to Troy and drives off. ἦ ῥα καί is ‘he spoke, and’; ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is a stock phrase for a hero, translated every time. ἄρνας are the lambs just killed. ἂν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔβαιν’ is ἀνέβαινε ‘went up’ with the preposition split from its verb (tmesis), and κατὰ δ’ … τεῖνεν is likewise κατέτεινεν ‘drew tight’, and the augment is kept in ἔβαιν’ (ἔ-βαινε) but absent in τεῖνεν; the same tmesis stands at 261 in the last part.

sentences.t: πὰρ δέ οἱ Ἀντήνωρ περικαλλέα βήσετο δίφρον.
sentences.l: and beside him Antenor the very beautiful chariot mounted;
sentences.i: and beside him Antenor stepped up into the very beautiful chariot;
sentences.n: Antenor, who came out with Priam, climbs in beside him. πὰρ is παρά ‘beside’, with οἱ ‘him’; περικαλλέα is ‘very beautiful’ (περί ‘exceedingly’, κάλλος ‘beauty’), agreeing with δίφρον ‘chariot’, and βήσετο is the epic aorist middle of βαίνω ‘mount’. This is the line at 262 again, translated the same way.

sentences.t: τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ἄψορροι προτὶ Ἴλιον ἀπονέοντο·
sentences.l: And the two, returning, to Ilios were going away;
sentences.i: And the two went away, returning to Ilios;
sentences.n: The old men leave the plain. τώ is the dual article ‘the two’, ἄψορροι an adjective ‘going back, returning’, agreeing with it, and ἀπονέοντο the imperfect of ἀπονέομαι ‘go back’. Priam and Antenor are out of the story for the rest of the part.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ Πριάμοιο πάϊς καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
χῶρον μὲν πρῶτον διεμέτρεον, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
κλήρους ἐν κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ πάλλον ἑλόντες,
ὁππότερος δὴ πρόσθεν ἀφείη χάλκεον ἔγχος.
sentences.l:
And Hector, Priam’s son, and heavenly Odysseus
the ground first measured out, and then
lots in a bronze-fitted helmet shook, having taken them,
to see which of the two should first let fly the bronze spear.
sentences.i: Hector, Priam’s son, and heavenly Odysseus first measured out the ground, and then took lots and shook them in a bronze-fitted helmet, to see which of the two should first let fly his bronze spear.
sentences.n: The Trojans and Achaeans each give a man to set the ground and draw the lots, Hector for Troy and Odysseus for the Achaeans. διεμέτρεον is the imperfect of διαμετρέω ‘measure out’, with its ending left uncontracted, and πάλλον ‘shook’ the imperfect of πάλλω. ὁππότερος δὴ πρόσθεν ἀφείη is an indirect question in the optative, ‘which of the two should first let fly’ (ἀφίημι). κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ is ‘a bronze-fitted helmet’, χαλκήρης ‘bronze-fitted’ is the word for the helmet here. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet.

sentences.t:
λαοὶ δ’ ἠρήσαντο, θεοῖσι δὲ χεῖρας ἀνέσχον,
ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε·
sentences.l:
And the people prayed, and to the gods lifted their hands,
and thus kept saying someone of the Achaeans and of the Trojans:
sentences.i: The troops prayed and held up their hands to the gods, and thus would some man, Achaean or Trojan, say:
sentences.n: The armies, not their leaders, now pray. λαοί is ‘the people’ of an army; ἠρήσαντο is the aorist middle of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, and ἀνέσχον the aorist of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’. The second line is 297 again, and so is its English.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ Ἴδηθεν μεδέων κύδιστε μέγιστε
ὁππότερος τάδε ἔργα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔθηκε,
τὸν δὸς ἀποφθίμενον δῦναι δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
ἡμῖν δ’ αὖ φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ γενέσθαι.
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, from Ida ruling, most glorious, greatest,
whichever of the two has set these deeds among both sides,
him grant, having perished, to go down into the house of Hades,
and for us in turn friendship and faithful oaths to come to be.”
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious, greatest, whichever of the two has brought these deeds upon both sides, grant that he perish and go down into the house of Hades, and that friendship and faithful oaths may come to be for us.”
sentences.n: The armies’ prayer asks that the man who began the quarrel should die and that peace follow. The first line is the address of 276, with the same English; ὁππότερος ‘whichever of the two’ means the two champions, and τάδε ἔργα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔθηκε is ‘has set these deeds among both sides’. τὸν δὸς ἀποφθίμενον δῦναι is ‘grant that he, having perished, go down’ (ἀποφθίνω, δῦναι the aorist infinitive of δύω). The two infinitives δῦναι and γενέσθαι both hang on δός ‘grant’; φιλότητα ‘friendship’ and ὅρκια πιστά ‘faithful oaths’ are the peace the oaths bring.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν, πάλλεν δὲ μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
ἂψ ὁρόων·
sentences.l:
So then they spoke, and shook the lots great Hector of the glancing helmet,
looking backward;
sentences.i: So they spoke, and great Hector of the glancing helmet shook the lots, looking backward;
sentences.n: Hector draws the lot. ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so then they spoke’, closing the prayers, and πάλλεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πάλλω ‘shake’; the lots, the object, are supplied from 316. ἂψ ὁρόων ‘looking backward’ is Hector with his face turned away. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet (κόρυς ‘helmet’, αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’), translated every time.

sentences.t: Πάριος δὲ θοῶς ἐκ κλῆρος ὄρουσεν.
sentences.l: and Paris’ lot swiftly sprang out.
sentences.i: and Paris’ lot sprang out quickly.
sentences.n: Πάριος is an adjective ‘of Paris’, and Paris is Alexander, the same man. ἐκ … ὄρουσεν is a tmesis, ‘sprang out’ of the helmet, and θοῶς ‘swiftly’ is the adverb of θοός. By the rule set at 316–317, the lot that leaps out first decides who throws first.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἔπειθ’ ἵζοντο κατὰ στίχας, ἧχι ἑκάστῳ
ἵπποι ἀερσίποδες καὶ ποικίλα τεύχε’ ἔκειτο·
sentences.l:
And the men then sat down in their ranks, where for each
the foot-lifting horses and the intricate armour lay;
sentences.i: Then the men sat down in their ranks, each where his high-stepping horses and intricate armour lay;
sentences.n: The armies take their seats while the champions arm. ἵζοντο is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit down’, κατὰ στίχας ‘in ranks’, and ἧχι ἑκάστῳ ‘where for each’. ἀερσίποδες, built on ἀείρω ‘lift’ and πούς ‘foot’, is an epithet of horses and is usually taken to mean ‘lifting the feet high’; the sense is not quite certain. ποικίλα τεύχεα is ‘intricate armour’, ποικίλος ‘of varied, intricate work’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἐδύσετο τεύχεα καλὰ
δῖος Ἀλέξανδρος Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο.
sentences.l:
And he, around his shoulders, put on his fine armour,
heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen.
sentences.i: And heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen, put the fine armour about his shoulders.
sentences.n: The arming of Alexander is told piece by piece, in a fixed order: greaves, breastplate, sword, shield, helmet, spear. ἐδύσετο is an aorist middle of δύω ‘put on’, and τεύχεα καλά is ‘fine armour’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ and ἠΰκομος ‘fine-haired’ are stock epithets, translated every time, even of Paris.

sentences.t:
κνημῖδας μὲν πρῶτα περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκε
καλάς, ἀργυρέοισιν ἐπισφυρίοις ἀραρυίας·
sentences.l:
Greaves first about his shins he set,
fine ones, with silver ankle-clasps fitted;
sentences.i: First he set fine greaves about his shins, fitted with silver ankle-clasps;
sentences.n: The first piece of armour is the greaves. κνημῖδες are the shin-guards, the thing named in ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’; ἐπισφύρια are the clasps at the ankle that hold them on, and ἀραρυίας is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, agreeing with κνημῖδας. πρῶτα ‘first’ opens the sequence that δεύτερον ‘second’ continues.

sentences.t:
δεύτερον αὖ θώρηκα περὶ στήθεσσιν ἔδυνεν
οἷο κασιγνήτοιο Λυκάονος·
sentences.l:
Second, in turn, a breastplate about his chest he put on,
of his own brother Lycaon;
sentences.i: Second, he put on about his chest the breastplate of his own brother Lycaon;
sentences.n: The breastplate is not Alexander’s own. θώρηξ is the breastplate, δεύτερον αὖ ‘second, in turn’; οἷο is the possessive pronoun in the genitive, ‘of his own’, and κασιγνήτοιο Λυκάονος ‘of his brother Lycaon’ names whose it was. ἔδυνεν is the imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἥρμοσε δ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l: and it fitted him.
sentences.i: and it fitted him.
sentences.n: That a borrowed breastplate fits is worth saying, and the poet says it. ἥρμοσε is the aorist of ἁρμόζω ‘fit’, here intransitive, and αὐτῷ ‘him, himself’ is its dative.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετο ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
χάλκεον, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε·
sentences.l:
and about his shoulders he slung the silver-studded sword,
bronze, and then the shield, great and stout;
sentences.i: and slung about his shoulders the silver-studded sword, a bronze one, and then the shield, great and stout;
sentences.n: The sword and the shield. ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον ‘silver-studded sword’ is a stock phrase, with ἧλος ‘stud, nail’ inside the compound, and χάλκεον ‘of bronze’ says what the blade is made of. σάκος is the shield, μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε ‘great and stout’ describing it. βάλετο is the aorist middle of βάλλω, ‘threw about himself, slung’. The same line stands at 2.45, and l has the same English there.

sentences.t:
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ ἰφθίμῳ κυνέην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκεν
ἵππουριν·
sentences.l:
and on his mighty head the well-made helmet he placed,
horse-tailed;
sentences.i: and on his mighty head he placed the well-made helmet, with its horsetail plume;
sentences.n: The helmet, with its plume of horsehair. κρατί is the epic dative of κάρη ‘head’; ἰφθίμῳ ‘mighty’ is the stock epithet and εὔτυκτον ‘well-made’. ἵππουριν is ἵππος ‘horse’ with οὐρά ‘tail’, ‘horse-tailed’: a crest of horsehair. Both lines are also in the Odyssey, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: δεινὸν δὲ λόφος καθύπερθεν ἔνευεν·
sentences.l: and fearsomely the crest above nodded;
sentences.i: and fearsomely the crest nodded above;
sentences.n: The crest of the helmet moves with every motion of the head. δεινόν is an adverb, ‘fearsomely’, and the Odyssey’s wording of the same half-line is kept; ἔνευεν is the imperfect of νεύω ‘nod’ (the final ν is movable), and καθύπερθεν ‘from above’. The crest is the λόφος.

sentences.t: εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος, ὅ οἱ παλάμηφιν ἀρήρει.
sentences.l: and he took up a sturdy spear, which to his palm was fitted.
sentences.i: and he took up his sturdy spear, which fitted his hand.
sentences.n: The last piece, the spear. ἄλκιμον ‘sturdy’ is the stock epithet; ὅ οἱ is the relative ὅ ‘which’ with οἱ ‘to him’, and παλάμηφιν is the old ending -φιν serving as a dative, ‘to his palm’. ἀρήρει is the pluperfect of ἀραρίσκω ‘was fitted’. The same words appear in the Odyssey at the start of a longer sentence.

sentences.t: ὣς δ’ αὔτως Μενέλαος ἀρήϊος ἔντε’ ἔδυνεν.
sentences.l: And just so warlike Menelaus put on his gear.
sentences.i: And in just the same way warlike Menelaus put on his gear.
sentences.n: Menelaus arms in the same sequence, which the poet does not repeat. ὣς δ’ αὔτως is ‘and just so’; ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet here, and ἔντε’ is ἔντεα ‘gear, equipment’ with its last vowel elided. ἔδυνεν is ‘put on’ as at 332.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ἑκάτερθεν ὁμίλου θωρήχθησαν,
ἐς μέσσον Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ἐστιχόωντο
δεινὸν δερκόμενοι·
sentences.i: And when the two had armed themselves on either side of the throng, they marched into the middle, between the Trojans and the Achaeans, with dread looks;
sentences.n: The two champions come out between the armies. οἳ δ’ here is the pair, and ἑκάτερθεν ὁμίλου ‘on either side of the throng’ puts each of them at the edge of his own army; θωρήχθησαν is the aorist passive of θωρήσσω ‘arm’. Line 341 is the line at 266 repeated, with the same English. δεινὸν δερκόμενοι ‘looking dreadfully’ has δεινόν as an adverb, from δεινός ‘dread’, and δέρκομαι ‘look’.

sentences.t:
θάμβος δ’ ἔχεν εἰσορόωντας
Τρῶάς θ’ ἱπποδάμους καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
and wonder held those looking on,
the horse-taming Trojans and the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: and wonder held them as they looked on, the Trojans, tamers of horses, and the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: The spectators are struck dumb. θάμβος ‘wonder’, the noun of θαμβέω, is the feeling that held them; εἰσορόωντας is the accusative plural participle of εἰσοράω ‘look on’, agreeing with Τρῶας and Ἀχαιούς. ἱππόδαμοι ‘horse-taming’ is the stock epithet of Trojans and ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ of Achaeans, translated every time.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἐγγὺς στήτην διαμετρητῷ ἐνὶ χώρῳ
σείοντ’ ἐγχείας ἀλλήλοισιν κοτέοντε.
sentences.l:
And they stood near, in the measured-out ground,
shaking their spears at one another, both bearing a grudge.
sentences.i: And the two stood close to each other, within the measured ground, shaking their spears at one another, each bearing a grudge.
sentences.n: The two are in position, close together. στήτην is the dual aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, and σείοντε and κοτέοντε are dual participles, ‘the two shaking’, ‘the two bearing a grudge’ (κοτέω); ἐγχείας is the accusative plural of ἐγχείη, ‘spear’, a by-form of ἔγχος, and the form is σείοντ’, elided. διαμετρητῷ ‘measured out’ is a rare adjective from the verb of 315, and the ground is the one marked off there.

sentences.t:
πρόσθε δ’ Ἀλέξανδρος προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλεν Ἀτρεΐδαο κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσε ἴσην,
οὐδ’ ἔρρηξεν χαλκός, ἀνεγνάμφθη δέ οἱ αἰχμὴ
ἀσπίδ’ ἐνὶ κρατερῇ·
sentences.l:
In front Alexander sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and hit the son of Atreus on the shield, equal on every side,
and the bronze did not break it, and its point was bent back
in the strong shield;
sentences.i: Alexander was first to send forth his long-shadowed spear, and he hit the son of Atreus on his shield, equal on every side; the bronze did not break it, and its point was bent back in the strong shield;
sentences.n: Alexander throws first, as the lot decided. προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ is the stock epithet of the spear, and the English of the Odyssey for it is kept. Ἀτρεΐδαο is Menelaus (the genitive in -αο). πάντοσε ἴσην ‘equal on every side’ describes a shield perfectly round; οὐδ’ ἔρρηξεν χαλκός ‘the bronze did not break it’ has the shield as an understood object. ἀνεγνάμφθη is the aorist passive of ἀναγνάμπτω ‘bend back’, and the point (αἰχμή) bends back instead of piercing.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ δεύτερον ὄρνυτο χαλκῷ
Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος ἐπευξάμενος Διὶ πατρί·
sentences.l:
and he in second place rushed on with the bronze,
Atreus’-son Menelaus, having prayed to father Zeus:
sentences.i: and Menelaus, son of Atreus, rushed on second with the bronze, after praying to father Zeus:
sentences.n: Menelaus now has his turn, and prays before he throws. ὄρνυτο ‘rose, rushed’ is the verb of 267, here with χαλκῷ ‘with the bronze’ (the spear), and δεύτερον ‘second’ answers πρόσθε ‘first’ at 346. Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος names which son of Atreus is meant; ἐπευξάμενος is the aorist participle of ἐπεύχομαι ‘pray’.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ ἄνα δὸς τίσασθαι ὅ με πρότερος κάκ’ ἔοργε
δῖον Ἀλέξανδρον, καὶ ἐμῇς ὑπὸ χερσὶ δάμασσον,
ὄφρα τις ἐρρίγῃσι καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἀνθρώπων
ξεινοδόκον κακὰ ῥέξαι, ὅ κεν φιλότητα παράσχῃ.
sentences.l:
“Zeus, lord, grant to take vengeance on him who first did evil to me,
heavenly Alexander, and beneath my hands subdue him,
so that someone may shudder, even of men born later,
to do evil to a host, whoever may offer friendship.”
sentences.i: “Lord Zeus, grant that I take vengeance on him who first did me evil, heavenly Alexander, and subdue him beneath my hands, so that even among men born later someone may shudder to do evil to a host who offers friendship.”
sentences.n: Menelaus asks for vengeance, and states what the wrong was: harm done to a host. ἄνα is the short vocative of ἄναξ ‘lord’; δὸς τίσασθαι is ‘grant to take vengeance’, with the person (Ἀλέξανδρον) as object of the middle verb, and ἔοργε is the perfect of ῥέζω ‘do’. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet, translated every time even of the man he hates. ὄφρα … ἐρρίγῃσι is a purpose clause with the perfect subjunctive of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, and ὀψιγόνων ‘born later’ are men of the future. ξεινοδόκον, ‘host’, is the man who receives a guest; the wrong is a guest’s wrong against his host.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλε Πριαμίδαο κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσε ἴσην·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and having brandished it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and hit the son of Priam on the shield, equal on every side;
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit the son of Priam on his shield, equal on every side;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ cast. ἦ ῥα καί is ‘he spoke, and’; ἀμπεπαλών is the aorist participle of ἀναπάλλω ‘swing back, brandish’, and the second half-line is the one at 346 with the same English. Πριαμίδαο ‘son of Priam’ is Paris, a patronymic that mirrors Ἀτρεΐδαο at 347; βάλε is the unaugmented aorist ‘hit’.

sentences.t:
διὰ μὲν ἀσπίδος ἦλθε φαεινῆς ὄβριμον ἔγχος,
καὶ διὰ θώρηκος πολυδαιδάλου ἠρήρειστο·
sentences.l:
Through the shining shield went the mighty spear,
and through the much-wrought breastplate it was driven;
sentences.i: The mighty spear went through the shining shield, and was driven through the richly wrought breastplate as well;
sentences.n: The spear goes through both layers of Paris’ protection. φαεινῆς ‘shining’ is the stock epithet of the shield, ὄβριμον ‘mighty’ of the spear, and πολυδαιδάλου ‘much-wrought’ (‘richly wrought’ in English) is built on δαίδαλος ‘cunningly made’. ἠρήρειστο is the pluperfect passive of ἐρείδω ‘drive, press’, ‘was driven in’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the short ι of διὰ is lengthened in the first foot.

sentences.t:
ἀντικρὺ δὲ παραὶ λαπάρην διάμησε χιτῶνα
ἔγχος·
sentences.l:
and straight on, along the flank, it cut through the tunic,
the spear;
sentences.i: and straight on, along his flank, the spear cut through the tunic;
sentences.n: The spear has gone through shield and breastplate, and now cuts Paris’ tunic along his side. ἀντικρύ ‘straight on’, παραί here is παρά ‘along’ with the accusative λαπάρην ‘flank’, and διάμησε is the aorist of διαμάω ‘cut through’. The subject, ἔγχος ‘the spear’, is held to the start of the next line. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐκλίνθη καὶ ἀλεύατο κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.l: but he leaned away and avoided the black death-fate.
sentences.i: but he swerved aside and avoided the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: Paris escapes: ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is Paris, not Menelaus. ἐκλίνθη is the aorist passive of κλίνω ‘lean, bend’, so ‘leaned away’; ἀλεύατο is the aorist middle of ἀλεύομαι ‘avoid’, and κῆρα μέλαιναν ‘the black death-fate’ (‘the black spirit of death’ in English) is a stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
πλῆξεν ἀνασχόμενος κόρυθος φάλον·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son, drawing his silver-studded sword,
struck, raising himself, the ridge of the helmet;
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus drew his silver-studded sword and, rising to the blow, struck the ridge of the helmet;
sentences.n: Menelaus, whose spear missed its man, attacks with the sword. Ἀτρεΐδης is Menelaus again, and ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον ‘silver-studded sword’ the same stock phrase used of Paris’ sword at 334. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, πλῆξεν the aorist of πλήσσω ‘strike’, and ἀνασχόμενος the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω, ‘raising himself’, here ‘rising to the blow’. φάλος is a part of the helmet, usually taken to be the ridge that carried the plume; its sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῷ
τριχθά τε καὶ τετραχθὰ διατρυφὲν ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.l:
and about it
in three pieces and in four, shattered, it fell from his hand.
sentences.i: and around it the sword was shattered into three pieces and four and fell from his hand.
sentences.n: The sword breaks on the helmet. ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῷ ‘and about it’ means about the helmet; τριχθά τε καὶ τετραχθά ‘in three pieces and in four’ is a Greek way of saying ‘into several pieces’. διατρυφέν is the aorist passive participle of διαθρύπτω ‘break in pieces’, neuter, agreeing with the understood ξίφος ‘sword’, and ἔκπεσε is the aorist of ἐκπίπτω ‘fall out’, with χειρός ‘from his hand’ in the genitive of separation.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ᾤμωξεν ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν·
sentences.l: And Atreus’-son wailed, looking to the wide heaven:
sentences.i: And the son of Atreus cried out, looking up to the wide heaven:
sentences.n: Menelaus turns on Zeus, whom he looked to for help at 351. Ἀτρεΐδης is Menelaus; ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘wail, cry out in grief’, and εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘to the wide heaven’ shows that the speech is addressed upward. εὐρύς ‘wide’ is the stock epithet of heaven.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ οὔ τις σεῖο θεῶν ὀλοώτερος ἄλλος·
sentences.l: “Father Zeus, none of the gods is deadlier than you, none other;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, no other god is deadlier than you;
sentences.n: The complaint opens with the same address as the prayers, and turns it into an accusation. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ ‘you’, used for comparison after ὀλοώτερος, the comparative of ὀλοός ‘baneful, deadly’, and ἄλλος ‘other’ at the end says the same thing again for emphasis. The line is a line of the Odyssey, with the same English.

sentences.t: ἦ τ’ ἐφάμην τίσασθαι Ἀλέξανδρον κακότητος·
sentences.l: Truly I thought to take vengeance on Alexander for his baseness;
sentences.i: Truly I thought I would take vengeance on Alexander for his baseness;
sentences.n: What he had hoped, and what has happened instead. ἦ τ’ ἐφάμην ‘truly I thought’ (ἐφάμην the imperfect middle of φημί), and τίσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of τίνομαι ‘take vengeance on’, with the person as object and the thing in the genitive: κακότητος ‘for his baseness’, the noun of κακός. Same verb as at 351.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ μοι ἐν χείρεσσιν ἄγη ξίφος, ἐκ δέ μοι ἔγχος
ἠΐχθη παλάμηφιν ἐτώσιον, οὐδ’ ἔβαλόν μιν.
sentences.l:
but now in my hands my sword is broken, and from me the spear
darted from my palm in vain, and I did not hit him.”
sentences.i: but now my sword is broken in my hands, and my spear darted from my palm in vain, and I did not hit him.”
sentences.n: He counts what the cast and the blow have come to. ἄγη is the aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’ with its augment lost (Attic ἐάγη), and ἠΐχθη the aorist passive of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’; ἐκ … παλάμηφιν ‘from the palm’ with the old -φιν ending as in 338. ἐτώσιον ‘in vain’ is neuter, used as an adverb, and οὐδ’ ἔβαλόν μιν is ‘and I did not hit him’, with μιν ‘him’, Paris. The speech ends here.
